articles.title: A year after Israeli strikes killed journalists at a hospital, no one has been held accountable
articles.summary: Rights groups say Israel rarely holds troops accountable for killing Palestinians, pointing to long investigations that rarely lead to prosecution.
articles.body: TEL AVIV — It’s been a year since Israeli soldiers killed 22 Palestinians, including journalists and rescue workers, in a double strike on a hospital in Gaza. No one has been held accountable. Israeli officials said the target was a suspected Hamas camera on the roof of Nasser Hospital. Among those killed were Reuters cameraman Hussam al-Masri and Mariam Dagga, a visual journalist who worked for The Associated Press and other news organizations. Despite repeated requests by AP, the army hasn’t provided details about the investigation or a timeline for when it could be completed. Rights groups say Israel rarely holds troops accountable for killing Palestinians, pointing to long investigations that rarely lead to prosecution. As global outrage over the Aug. 25, 2025, strikes grew, the Israeli military said that in addition to taking out the camera, six of those killed were linked to Hamas, without providing evidence. But an Israeli soldier, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution, now says the military could find no evidence linking the camera, which belonged to al-Masri, to Hamas. The soldier, who was privy to discussions surrounding the military’s response, said none of the six was the intended target of the strikes. AP sent detailed questions to the military about the allegations, as well as other questions about the strikes. The military didn’t address the questions but said the incident is being examined and findings will be transferred to the Military Advocate General’s Corps to reach a verdict on whether to open a criminal investigation. It didn’t provide a timeline. The army said it would not comment on details while the incident was under review. AP reported at the time that one of the six Israel said was linked to Hamas wasn’t on the hospital’s list of casualties and two others were medical or emergency personnel. That, along with the soldier’s account, raises serious questions about Israel’s rationale for the strikes. Why did troops fail to identify the cameraman as al-Masri, even though journalists were known to film at the hospital? Why did they strike a second time, causing most of the deaths and raising accusations of a “double tap” attack on first responders, which would be a war crime? AP and Reuters released a statement Tuesday calling again for Israel to provide a full explanation of the strikes. The news organizations also called on Israel to give journalists access to Gaza to support colleagues who have covered the war from the beginning. “A year later, we remain devastated by their deaths and are still searching for answers from the Israeli authorities about what happened,” the statement read. Nasser Hospital was a vital location for journalists News agencies like Reuters and AP supplied live video footage to newsrooms around the world from the hospital, one of the few functioning in Gaza at the time. AP repeatedly informed the army that its journalists were there. The first strike killed al-Masri and another person. As other journalists, including Dagga, and rescue workers rushed up an external staircase to help the wounded and document what happened, the military struck again, killing 20. Based on footage and eyewitnesses, none was armed. In all, Israel struck the hospital four times using high-explosive tank shells. Israeli officials afterward said Hamas was using the camera to observe nearby troops. They alleged “suspicious behavior” around the camera, but the only example they gave was that a towel draped over the camera and the person filming appeared to be an effort at concealment. Al-Masri routinely covered equipment with a white cloth to protect it from the sun and dust, a common practice among journalists in Gaza and other hot climates. Last week, the army announced criminal investigations into two other high-profile attacks by its troops in Gaza — the 2024 killing of 5-year-old Hind Rajab and her family, and the 2025 killing of 15 paramedics. It cleared troops in three other attacks that killed international aid group workers. Soldier details an attempt at damage control The soldier was connected to AP through Breaking the Silence, a group founded over two decades ago by Israeli veterans that collects testimony from soldiers and is critical of Israel’s actions in the Palestinian territories. The soldier said after high-profile strikes that kill civilians without clear military purpose, army officials search for militant links among those killed. Breaking the Silence said its testimonies show there is a “retroactive incrimination process” in which Palestinians who are killed are automatically counted as militants, even when unarmed. Retroactive incrimination is used as a “near-automatic justification for every bullet, shell or missile fired, and as a tool used to avoid carrying out real investigations,” said Nadav Weiman, the group’s executive director. AP confirmed some details of the soldier’s account, which is consistent with the military’s public response. Breaking the Silence said it corroborated the account with its own sources. The Israeli military has raided or laid siege to hospitals throughout the war, accusing Hamas of using them as command centers and to hide fighters, though it’s provided evidence for only some of its claims. Hamas security men have been seen in hospitals during the war, controlling access to certain areas. Earlier this year, Doctors Without Borders suspended some operations at Nasser Hospital for several months after patients and staff reported seeing armed, masked men roaming parts of the building. Tank shells were fired after a drone failed The soldier and a former military official with knowledge of the situation said a high-ranking army official initially approved use of a precision weapon to take down the camera, but an attempt by drone failed for unknown reasons. The former official spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to talk to the media. The division commander then approved an alternative method, said the soldier, without saying what the method was. It’s unclear who made the decision to fire tank rounds, which can cause more damage than drone strikes. Oded Ailam, former head of the counterterrorism division in Israel’s Mossad spy service, said while commanders on the ground have a degree of freedom, they don’t have a “blank check.” “If the change is significant, particularly where it may affect the risk to civilians, it must remain within the authority, rules and intent of the original order, or require renewed approval,” he said. Israeli troops have killed over 200 journalists in the war Israeli troops have killed 207 Palestinian reporters in Gaza since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack ignited the war, according to the New York-based Committee to Protect Journalists. Israel has barred foreign journalists from entering Gaza, giving Palestinian journalists a critical role. Sara Qudah, CPJ’s Middle East and North Africa regional director, said Israel has a responsibility to conduct a prompt, transparent investigation. “When journalists can be killed without credible accountability, it becomes harder and more dangerous for the press to document conflicts and for the public to know what is happening,” she said. The lack of answers has been agonizing for families. Ezz al-Din al-Masri said he doesn’t understand why his brother, Hussam, was killed. “Unfortunately, we found that the blood of journalists in Gaza is cheap … as if the rules protecting journalists do not apply,” he said. Dagga, 33, had just taken her last photos before rushing up the stairs. Whenever her father, Riyad Abu Dagga, visits her grave, he carries her phone and camera — she always had them with her. He visits her apartment near Nasser Hospital and cries. “Had any of the daughters of the soldiers been killed unjustly, they would not have stayed silent,” he said of the Israelis. “They would want to know why.”

If you have money sitting in a traditional savings account , you may not be getting a competitive return on your balance.

Today, the national average savings account rate is just 0.38%, according to the FDIC. However, a good savings account rate is much higher; today's best high-yield savings accounts pay closer to 4% APY — more than 10 times the average.

Here's a closer look at what a good savings account rate looks like in 2026, and where to find the best rates available.

What is a good interest rate for a savings account?

A good savings account rate is one that not only beats the national average (which is currently 0.38%), but also helps your savings outpace inflation. Considering that the current inflation rate is 3.4%, a good savings account rate should be above this threshold — otherwise, your money will lose purchasing power over time.

The good news: It's possible to find high-yield savings accounts as high as 4% APY or more.

Here are a few high-yield savings accounts with exceptionally good interest rates:

The Growth Savings account from Forbright Bank gives new account holders the chance to earn up to 4.15% APY on their balance through the end of this year. After that, account holders earn a still-competitive rate of 3.85% APY.

There is no minimum deposit required to open this account. However, you must deposit at least $1,000 to qualify for the 0.30% APY boost.

Bask Bank's Interest Savings Account offers a standard rate of 3.75% APY. However, new customers can earn a 0.10% rate boost — and all customers can get an additional 0.25% rate boost — by completing qualifying activities. There are no monthly fees or minimum balance requirements.

How to get the best possible interest rate on your savings

If your current savings account interest rate isn't doing you any favors, switching to a different bank could make sense to get a better return.

Take some time to shop around and compare the best high-yield savings accounts to get an idea of what's available. In particular, you'll want to focus your research on online banks , which are more likely to offer high-yield options than traditional banks and credit unions.

Here are some factors you'll want to consider throughout the process.

The annual percentage yield (APY) of an account tells you how much interest you can earn in a year based on your balance. It's typically higher than the account's interest rate because it considers compound interest.

For example, say a bank advertises a savings account with an interest rate: 3.92% and daily compounding interest. The 3.92% interest rate is the base rate the bank pays on your balance. But because interest is added to your account every day, you also earn interest on the interest you've already earned. That compounding boosts your annual return to 4% APY.

For example, if you deposit $10,000 and leave it in the account for one year :

Without compounding (3.92% interest rate): You would earn about $392 in interest.

With daily compounding (4% APY): You would earn about $400, ending the year with $10,400.

In this example, the extra $8 comes solely from compounding.

Some financial institutions may have an initial deposit requirement when you open an account, as well as an ongoing minimum balance requirement. If you don't meet a balance requirement, you may be subject to a lower APY or even a monthly fee.

Minimum balance requirements may not be an issue if you have a sizable savings balance, but it may be worth it to avoid accounts with higher minimums to avoid the risk of getting a lower return.

With an online bank, you likely won't get the option to withdraw cash at a local branch. However, online banks typically offer the following ways to access your money:

Transfer to your checking account: If you're transferring the funds to an account with the same bank, it's instantaneous.

Transfer to an external account: If you keep your checking account with a separate bank, you can typically request a transfer and get the funds within a few days.

Withdraw from an ATM: Many online banks have large ATM networks, making it easy to get actual cash when you need it. That said, you'll want to check ATM withdrawal limits to ensure you won't have problems getting the amount you need.

It's important to note that some banks that offer high-yield savings accounts don't offer checking accounts or even ATM networks. In this case, the only option to get your money — an external bank transfer — can take a few days. That can be worth it if the APY is high and you're not concerned about needing funds quickly. However, it can be risky in the event of a financial emergency.

While it may seem natural to keep your checking and savings accounts with the same bank, some online banks only offer savings options. If your top priority is to earn the best rate on your savings, you may not mind maintaining accounts at separate banks.

However, if you'd rather have the convenience of having your checking and savings accounts with the same bank, ensure the financial institutions you're considering offer both.

You can also consider other financial products and services (such as loans, credit cards, and investment services) each bank offers to see if you can get more overall value by moving more than just your savings and checking funds.

An APY of 5% is excellent. Unfortunately, there are currently little to no savings accounts that offer rates this high. Most of the top savings account rates hover around 4%. That said, savings rates can fluctuate, so what qualifies as a good savings account interest rate is a moving target.

Where can I get 7% interest on my money online?

There aren't any major banks that currently offer a 7% interest rate on your savings, though it may be possible to find that kind of return on a portion of your balance with a small bank or credit union.

Remember, though, that savings account rates can change over time. If you want to maximize the return on your balance, shop around now and then to see if you can get a better rate than what your current financial institution offers.

articles.summary: The best nail strengtheners prevent nails from splitting, breaking or cracking. Here's how to shop for them with options from OPI, CND and more.
articles.body: There are plenty of skin care rituals to keep our faces, hands and feet looking their best. But, beyond the occasional manicure, our nails — composed of the same protein as our top layer of skin — often remain untreated, leading to frequent splitting and breaking. We spoke to nail experts about everything you need to know to nourish your natural nails properly, including their nail strengthener recommendations for healing damaged nails. We also included everything you need to know about the recent ban on gel nail polish products in Europe (more on that, and what it means for you and your nails, below). Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. The best nail strengtheners Brittle nails that crack or peel are not uncommon. In fact, Harvard Medical School suggests that over one in four women have onychoschizia, or nail fragility. Various factors like dehydration, nail-biting and even everyday tasks like typing can cause it. That being said, experts recommend nail strengtheners for people with nails that frequently split or crack. Deciding which one works best for you depends on several factors, including application type, frequency of use and price point. To help you, we’ve followed expert advice to round up some highly rated picks we love. Best overall This nail serum is designed to rebuild the damaged keratin bonds in your nails, which results in stronger and smoother nails, according to the brand. It uses maleic acid to penetrate the surface of the nails to help strengthen them from within, making them more resistant to breakage and giving them less ridges and better color. The serum is also formulated without formaldehyde or parabens. Best for nail growth Keratin is one of the essential proteins required for nail growth, which is why it’s a common ingredient in nail strengtheners and frequently recommended by our experts. This Nail-Aid treatment, a favorite of NBC Selected editorial director Lauren Swanson and associate SEO reporter Ashley Morris, facilitates nail growth in just a few days, especially when used regularly. Best for damaged nails Rita Remark, Essie’s global lead educator and nail artist, warns customers to steer clear of nail strengtheners that include formaldehyde. This nail strengthener from modelones is free from not only formaldehyde but other potentially toxic and weakening ingredients (including fragrances and phthalates) as well. Instead, the product relies on expert-recommended ingredients, including keratin and jojoba oil. Please note: Any Essie product recommendations were made independently of Remark. Best hand lotion Customers love this hand and nail lotion for its dual purpose — not only does it help to moisturize skin with Vaseline Jelly, it also contains mineral oil and keratin, two ingredients Green recommends in any nail strengthener. Several reviewers also cite a noticeable improvement in nail strength in a couple of weeks. Best base coat NBC Selected senior editor Nikki Brown loves acrylic tips, but when she’s ready to give her nails a rest, this Sally Hansen nail strengthener is her favorite product. “I like this one because it doubles as a clear polish, so my nails are naked but not that naked, and still getting the nourishment they need from the protein and silk formula,” she says. “Whenever I’m wearing this, my nails feel harder and break way less.” Best value cream Morris was introduced to this nail-strengthening cream by her roommate, who’s sworn by it for years. It has vitamins A, C, E and D, beeswax and jojoba oil to condition and nourish nails while moisturizing the skin around them, according to the brand. Morris says the formula isn’t drying, and that it smells like coconut instead of chemicals. Best oil This nail and cuticle oil is formulated to hydrate and soothe damaged cuticles, and helps nails to feel harder and stronger in as little as two weeks, according to the brand. Vitamin E, which Green notes is critical for healthier nails, is a primary ingredient, alongside jojoba oil, which helps lock in moisture over time. Best polish This well-known brand is a customer favorite. It can be used as either a standalone treatment or as a base coat underneath your manicure. Ingredients like hydrolyzed wheat protein and calcium help build stronger nails over time, while the variety of color options lets you maintain a stylish manicure as your nails heal. Best cream This nail cream works best when applied a couple of times daily, says the brand. Its main ingredient, lanolin, has been found to reduce the amount of water lost through the skin by up to 30%, which in turn helps to prevent nail cracking and cuticle peeling. The conditioner is formulated to work for all levels of nail damage, and visibly improves nails in two to three weeks, according to the brand. Best vegan formula Vitamin E enhances this vegan and cruelty-free formula, which is made without harmful chemicals like acetone and formaldehyde. According to the brand, it can also be used underneath polish, but it may affect how long your manicure lasts. Best top coat You can use this Duri product as both a base coat and a top coat to help lock in moisture and provide a healthy dose of collagen and fatty acids—two expert-recommended ingredients for stronger, healthier nails. It’s especially great for those recovering from damage caused by acrylics and other nail extensions, according to the brand. Best for peeling This nail treatment from Orly works over 14 days to promote strong and healthy nail growth, according to the brand. It uses bamboo extract, green tea, hemp seed oil and vitamin C to help stop your nails from peeling, splitting and breaking, and is especially great for nails that’ve been damaged by acrylic or gel nails, according to the brand. How we picked the best nail strengtheners To pick the best nail strengtheners, we followed expert guidance and included only options with active healing ingredients, which are detailed below. “Nail strengtheners work by providing extra protection to your nails and helping them to become thicker and stronger over time,” says Dr. Randa Jaafar, who specializes in interventional pain and wrinkle reduction. “They contain ingredients such as calcium, magnesium and vitamins A, C and E, which help to nourish and protect the nail. When used regularly, these ingredients can help improve your nails’ overall strength and health.” While nails generally become weaker over time, with regular use, nail strengtheners can help to rebuild and revitalize your natural nails. How to shop for a nail strengthener When it comes to finding the right nail strengthener for you, experts say that there are a few ingredients to look for and avoid while shopping. “When looking for a nail strengthener, you should look for key ingredients such as calcium, magnesium and vitamins A, C and E,” says Dr. Jaafar. In addition to looking for certain nourishing ingredients, she recommends steering clear of nail polishes and other nail-strengthening products that contain harsh chemicals, which can damage nails. What are the best ingredients to look for in a nail strengthener? The best ingredients for nail strengtheners are a range of vitamins as well as calcium and magnesium. Learn more about each below. Calcium: Brittle bones and nails are often linked to calcium deficiencies, especially since calcium is a key mineral for stronger nails. Insufficient calcium intake could result in nails that break or chip more easily or become thinner over time.Magnesium: Given that magnesium is necessary for protein synthesis in your body (which nails need to grow), it isn’t surprising that this mineral is important for healthy nails. Folks with vertical ridges in their nails may even have a magnesium deficiency.Vitamin A: Vitamin A helps keep your nails hydrated and promotes nail growth, says Dr. Jaafar. In particular, vitamin A promotes the synthesis of keratin, which is what our nails are made of.Vitamin C: Collagen production in the body depends upon vitamin C intake, and the collagen protein helps build fingernails (hair and teeth). Insufficient vitamin C intake could result in more brittle nails or slower-growing nails.Vitamin E: Vitamin E is crucial for keeping your nails hydrated and protecting your cuticles. Our experts note that using vitamin E oil — especially around your nail bed and cuticle — can help to undo the damage done by polish use. What ingredients should be avoided in a nail strengthener? Experts recommend steering clean of formaldehyde, toluene, and dibutyl phthalate. Learn more about each below. Formaldehyde: Jaafar and the FDA warn that excessive use of products containing formaldehyde can make nails more brittle and likely to peel. Moreover, some folks have sensitivities to this compound, which could result in allergic reactions.Toluene: While toluene can help to keep your nail polish smooth upon application, the chemical has been linked to nervous system damage; so much so that the EU has restricted toluene inclusion in a range of beauty products, including nail polish.Dibutyl phthalate (DBP): While DBP can make nail polish more durable, some studies have linked the compound to endocrine issues, making it difficult for the body to produce hormones. As with toluene, the EU has banned DBP use in nail polish and other beauty products. We also ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Dr. Randa Jaafar, MD, is an anesthesiologist, interventional pain specialist, and the founder of FILD Studio, which focuses on precision wrinkle prevention.Thea Green MBE is the founder of Nails. INC. Since founding Nails. INC. in 1999, her brand portfolio has expanded to include INC.redible Cosmetics, My Mood, and Holler & Glow. Rita Remark is an editorial manicurist and educator in New York, and the lead nail artist for Essie. Her creations can be found on runways and fashion magazines, including Alexander Wang and Vogue Korea. Why trust NBC Selected? Lulu Chang is a freelancer based in Washington, DC and New York City. Ashley Morris is an associate SEO reporter for NBC Selected, covering skin care, wellness and more. For this piece, they interviewed nail experts on everything you need to know about nail strengtheners, including how to find the best one for you. articles.title: UN chief condemns Haiti gang attack that killed at least 47
articles.summary: UN Secretary General António Guterres has condemned a gang attack in Haiti that killed at least 47 people, including 22 who were reportedly executed at a chu...
articles.body:
UN Secretary General António Guterres has condemned a gang attack in Haiti that killed at least 47 people, including 22 who were reportedly executed at a church compound where they had sought shelter.

The attack took place at the weekend in Kenscoff, a community on the outskirts of the capital Port-au-Prince.

"The relentless gang attacks on communities and the loss of lives underscore the alarming security conditions in Haiti and reinforce the urgent need to intensify Haitian and international security efforts to counter gangs," Guterres' spokesman, Stéphane Dujarric, said in a statement on Tuesday.

Guterres also reiterated his call for Haitian authorities to "ensure that those responsible for such attacks are held accountable," including through specialized judicial units recently established with international support to investigate mass crimes.

According to the UN Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH), more than 50 people were also abducted and 22 injured in Sunday night's attack on Kenscoff, around 10 kilometres south of Port-au-Prince.

The attackers targeted the centre of the community, setting numerous homes on fire and storming a church compound where displaced people had sought shelter, broadcaster Radio Télé Galaxie reported.

The UN's Dujarric said it was believed that 22 of the victims were killed at the church complex.

Police eventually managed to push back the attackers and regain control of the area.

Haiti's transitional government confirmed the attack but did not provide a death toll. It described the violence as a "heinous criminal attack," placed security forces on the highest level of alert and deployed reinforcements.

Criminal gangs have been trying for years to seize control of Kenscoff because of the mountainous community's strategic location, which allows control over key road connections.

Kenscoff is also close to Pétion-Ville, a comparatively affluent suburb of the capital that is home to numerous institutions, embassies and banks.

The community lies at an altitude of around 2,000 metres and, thanks to its cooler climate, is considered a relatively desirable residential area in the Caribbean country, which has been plagued by poverty and violence.

Haiti has been without a president since the assassination of Jovenel Moïse in July 2021, while an already precarious security situation has spiralled out of control.

Violent gangs control more than 80% of Port-au-Prince and have increasingly expanded into other communities, terrorizing residents, raping women and recruiting children.

According to UN figures, armed gangs killed 2,300 people in Haiti in the first five months of this year alone. More than 1,100 others were injured and almost 100 abducted.

Haiti, the poorest country in the Americas, is due to hold elections on December 13, its first since 2016.

articles.title: Australian officials allege 3M knew for 50 years its firefighting products were toxic
articles.summary: The government alleges internal company documents discussed the chemicals' ability to remain in the human body.
articles.body:
Australia's federal government says U.S. manufacturing conglomerate 3M kept selling firefighting foam for decades even though the company allegedly knew the chemicals in it could harm people, animals, and the environment.

Those allegations appear in extensive federal court papers tied to Australia's lawsuit seeking more than 2 billion Australian dollars ($1.4 billion) from 3M and its Australian subsidiary, according to The Guardian .

The accusations add to growing scrutiny of corporate decisions that can leave communities grappling with pollution long after the products themselves are gone.

Attorney General Michelle Rowland confirmed that the government was taking 3M to court over PFAS pollution connected to 28 defense bases in Australia, The Guardian reported.

The government says 3M sold aqueous film-forming foam, or AFFF, that contained PFAS "forever chemicals," which then polluted soil and water and led to major environmental and economic harm.

The court papers argue that by 1973, 3M and its Australian operations should already have understood that the products posed potential dangers.

The government alleges internal company documents discussed toxicity and the chemicals' ability to remain in the human body and also raised possible concerns about kidney function, the immune system, fertility, puberty, and infant birth weight.

The filing says that when defense personnel watched product demonstrations in 1967 and 1968, company brochures still described the foam as "non-toxic," The Guardian reported.

3M also said the products were "non-irritating" to humans, would not damage grass, were biodegradable, and were "not expected to adversely affect the ecology of receiving streams in the vicinity of [their] use."

If the government's claims are upheld, it would mean the company continued to promote a hazardous product in reassuring terms even as contamination risks spread into everyday places such as groundwater, drains, and nearby land.

PFAS are used in a wide range of industrial and household products because they resist heat, grease, and water.

However, those same qualities also make them incredibly persistent in every sense.

Many do not break down easily, which is why they are often referred to as forever chemicals.

Australia banned three key PFAS chemicals in 2025 after years of concern over health risks and environmental contamination.

One of them, PFOA, has been identified as cancer-causing in humans.

The filing says affected sites have required contaminated soil to be removed and treated, and investigations around the bases have been underway since about 2011.

When companies describe products as safe or eco-friendly while concealing environmental concerns, the fallout can last for generations, part of a broader deceptive business practice known as " greenwashing ."

The Australian government says it has already devoted substantial sums to addressing the contamination.

According to the filing, more than 214 million Australian dollars ($153 million) has gone toward investigations, monitoring, remediation, and mitigation, and over 51 million Australian dollars ($36 million) toward research and evidence gathering.

The documents also mention legal settlements worth hundreds of millions of dollars for loss and damage, according to The Guardian.

Defense began phasing out PFAS chemicals in 2004 and stopped buying 3M's AFFF in 2003.

Even so, the filing says the chemicals have continued to leach from concrete, asphalt, soil, and sediment into groundwater and surface water, suggesting cleanup will continue.

A company spokesperson said that 3M never manufactured PFAS in Australia and had stopped selling the products at issue, while defense continued to use them.

During a hearing in Melbourne, Federal Court Justice Catherine Button commented on the scale of the dispute, saying she had "never seen a claim like this," The Guardian reported.

She added that describing the case as daunting "would be an understatement."

articles.title: A British Army commander testing war robots says they aren't always the right tool for the job
articles.summary: Uncrewed ground vehicles, or UGVs, can present logistics, power, navigation, and control challenges for soldiers, he said.
articles.body:
A British Army commander says ground robots can be useful but come with drawbacks.

UGVs can create logistics, power, navigation, and control challenges for troops.

Ukraine shows their value may be mainly in dangerous, specialized missions that protect soldiers.

The commander of a British Army battalion tasked with experimenting with new technologies said that his unit has tested out dozens of ground robots. He concluded that they can be useful, but only for certain missions. And they come with a long list of challenges.

As Western militaries rush to absorb lessons from the war in Ukraine and integrate more uncrewed systems into their respective forces, soldiers are finding that some systems might look good on paper but aren't effective in all combat scenarios.

Ground robots , in particular, can face weight, navigation, cost, and power constraints that raise questions about when and how they should be used. In Ukraine's case, the systems have seen use in logistics operations, replacing soldiers in highly dangerous areas of the battlefield, but soldiers have also said they're not a catch-all solution.

At a recent US Army-led exercise at Fort Irwin in California, a handful of American allies and partners gathered with US forces to experiment with new systems in a simulated conflict against a near-peer adversary. The British Army's experimentation unit, the 2nd Battalion, The Yorkshire Regiment, was present for the event alongside the unit that will take over their experimentation role, the 1st Battalion Irish Guards.

During the recent exercise, Lt. Col. John Black, commander of the 2nd Battalion of the Yorkshire Regiment, told Business Insider that he and his unit have seen and tested a wide range of uncrewed ground vehicles, or UGVs.

"Any use case you can think of, we've tried it," he said, adding that they're not just driving it around to see how it works; rather, they are focused on "trying to employ it in a tactical scenario."

Through that experimentation, Black and his troops have encountered problems that can make UGVs difficult to use. For instance, many of the medium- to large-sized UGVs they tested required trailers or flatbed trucks to transport. Depending on how soldiers are moving and what they're carrying, that creates a logistical burden.

And once they've moved it into position, troops still have to figure out how to get it into the fight.

"Even if they've got quite long range and good speed, there's still going to be a process where you're moving them into the fight," Black said.

UGVs can also create power and refueling challenges. Depending on the system, specifically it's size, range, and capabilities, troops in the field may need to carry extra batteries, generators, or fuel — or periodically bring the robot back to a charging point.

Remote control introduces another set of problems, from maintaining a reliable connection to keeping the robot on course. The systems can also struggle with difficult terrain .

Often, their advertised range doesn't translate cleanly to real-world conditions, such as uneven ground. Obstacles "confound" most UGVs, Black said.

Whether UGVs can rely on autonomous features is a particularly thorny subject. Autonomy has become a major area of interest across uncrewed capabilities, but Black said some manufacturers have moved away from offering autonomous UGVs.

"We have seen, over the last few years, these vendors stop offering autonomous ones because it's unworkable," he said, explaining that such autonomous features can result in the system being more expensive and difficult to use.

Despite those limitations, Black said there are certain situations where he sees value, including breaches and mine removal .

Both missions are incredibly dangerous for soldiers. For that reason, militaries have been using remote-controlled technologies for breaching fortified positions and removing mines for decades. Certain UGVs coming online now could be the next evolution in that technology, but other methods could prove more practical.

Ground robots are seeing growing use in Ukraine, sometimes operating as a safer option than sending soldiers into "the kill zone" to deliver supplies and ammo. Ukraine has also used them offensively, such as driving one equipped with a gun off a drone boat in a first-of-its-kind robotic amphibious assault.

However, their growing use in that fight hasn't settled the debate on their overall usefulness. Black indicated that they might be a niche tool, most effective only in those cases where keeping a soldier out of harm's way matters most.

articles.title: Of 27 lakh âlogical discrepancyâ deletions in West Bengal, only 7 lakh appealed
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: In a new twist to the simmering controversy over the West Bengal SIR, Supreme Court was informed Tuesday that against 27-lakh odd deletions.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a new twist to the simmering controversy over the West Bengal SIR, Supreme Court was informed Tuesday that against 27-lakh odd deletions from votersâ list because of âlogical discrepancyâ only seven lakh filed appeals seeking inclusion of their names in the electoral rolls.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was informed by senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan that of total 38.1 lakh appeals filed before the SIR appellate tribunals, an overwhelming 31 lakh were filed by those who challenged inclusion of names in the rolls claiming they were ineligible to be voters in Bengal.Chunk of WB appeals was against inclusionThis was new information for SC, which was concerned by pendency of 37 lakh appeals, as 19 tribunals in last four months decided only 82,000 appeals. The new turn means 20 lakh of 27-lakh-odd voters deleted for logical discrepancy have not appealed against being struck off the rolls during the SIR.SC said a chunk of appeals was by those challenging inclusion. EC will give breakup differentiating those seeking inclusion from exclusion. Prioritising inclusion appeals would considerably reduce burden on tribunals, it said.For petitioner Prasenjit Bose from Congress, advocates Gopal Sankaranarayanan and Neha Rathi alleged that bulk of appeals for exclusion/deletion have been filed by EC in a mechanical manner against orders of judicial officers who had directed inclusion of the names and these appeals should not be heard at all.Sankaranarayanan said Kolkata and Howrah civic polls are due in Dec and at least appeals pertaining to these areas should be decided expeditiously so nobody gets disenfranchised illegally.SC said its main concern was expeditious decision on appeals of disenfranchised people. It directed EC to respond with data on appeals pending after segregating them into two categories â those seeking inclusion and those seeking exclusion of names. It asked EC to suggest a mechanism for speeding up disposal, including increasing the number of tribunals.The bench also asked EC to detail steps taken to include names of those whose appeals had been allowed. EC said it was holding meetings with the acting CJ of Calcutta HC and would submit a proposal on expediting disposal.Appearing for some petitioners, advocate Rauf Rahim said people whose names were deleted and whose appeals were pending should not be deprived of ration and benefits under the govt schemes.Advocate Kalyan Bandopadhyay told the bench that in Murshidabad, many constituencies had voter deletions far exceeding winning margin, and alleged a particular community appeared to have been targeted through SIR. articles.title: Texas Roadhouse says claims of white employees discussing spitting in Black customers' food in a Facebook group are 'completely unfounded'
articles.summary: US News: Texas Roadhouse clapped back at the viral social media claim that its white servers were discussing spitting in Black customers' food in a private Fac.
articles.body: Texas Roadhouse clapped back at the viral social media claim that its white servers were discussing spitting in Black customers' food in a private Facebook group as a hoax and confirmed that the claims based on which diners raised boycott calls were completely unfounded. The controversy started when an unverified claim originated on Facebook, allegedly from a user warning Black diners to avoid eating at Texas Roadhouse and Logan's Roadhouse. The post alleged that a secret Facebook group boasting over 400,000 white server members existed for the explicit purpose of organizing food contamination targeted at Black customers. Specific accusations claimed that servers were licking their fingers, spitting in saliva, and touching items like the chain's famous fresh rolls before serving them.The controversy escalated as the post went viral and customers called for a nationwide boycott."We are committed to creating an environment where every guest is treated with respect and unreasonable hospitality," Texas Roadhouse officials wrote responding to the outrage. "We do not tolerate discrimination, harassment or mistreatment of any kind, and we expect our Roadies to treat every guest with dignity and care."Texas Roadhouse brought in an independent third-party cybersecurity firm to trace the origins of the post. They confirmed there was no evidence of such a 400,000-member group existing, nor any record of food-tampering incidents linked to the claim.Travis Doster, chief communications officer of Texas Roadhouse, told USA TODAY that some social media users who defamed the chain retracted their statements after it was proved to be a hoax."Thereâs no video of any of our servers," he said. "Thereâs no video of anybody saying they have evidence. Itâs very frustrating because itâs not true." He also suggested the culprit behind the post could be bots, or automated programs that make posts mimicking human engagement online. "There is zero credible evidence this is true,â he said. âThis did not happen in any of our restaurants."Viral post deleted after creating outrageThe original Facebook post was deleted. It was allegedly shared in a Facebook group called "White and proud," where a user named Nancy Smith said they worked at an unidentified Texas Roadhouse location and was in a pact with other White servers at the restaurant to contaminate the food of Black guests.The user said this had been going on for a while, or at least since the April 2025 killing of 17-year-old Austin Metcalf by Black teenager Karmelo Anthony. articles.title: New US sanctions signal Trump desperation on Iran, experts say
articles.summary: Economic escalation is unlikely to force the Iranian government to capitulate to US demands, according to experts.
articles.body:
The United States announced new sanctions on Iran and a slew of global entities doing business with the country on Monday, in what officials have called an “economic D-Day” and officially dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast”, in an effort to force Tehran to negotiate an end to the war.

The announcement followed repeated demands by US President Donald Trump that Iranian leaders take actions like dropping their claims over the Strait of Hormuz and return to talks to end its nuclear programme.

list 1 of 3 Trump’s latest wave of Iran sanctions: Which 60 entities are targeted?

list 2 of 3 US launches Economic war on Iran

list 3 of 3 Sanctions or missiles? How Gulf will view Trump’s new Iran approach

Nearly six months into its war on Iran, the US is seeing little impact from its military operations against the country. Crucial military munitions stocks have been depleted, and important tools used to project power globally have been redirected towards Iran.

The long-term implications of the war, analysts say, have pushed the Trump administration to try economic sanctions, but these are unlikely to compel Iran into meeting the demands.

“The United States is returning to economic pressure because military force has failed to deliver the quick victory it expected,” Negar Mortazavi, senior fellow at the US-based Center for International Policy, told Al Jazeera. “The ‘economic D-Day’ declaration underscores the war’s failure so far to force Iran’s surrender or achieve Washington’s political objectives.”

“On paper, the US and Iran are a huge military mismatch,” Ryan Costello, policy director at the National Iranian American Council (NIAC), told Al Jazeera. “The US caused a lot of destruction with its munitions, but so too did Iran with its missiles and drones. So it is hard to describe the war to date as anything but a catastrophic mistake.”

While the US has killed key Iranian political and military leaders, Tehran has leveraged its geography and vast arsenal of drones and missiles, striking out at key oil and gas infrastructure in a region that has depended on drawing investors by offering stability. And Tehran’s choking of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has brought pain for consumers as far away as the US, who now pay about 40 percent more at the petrol pump than before the war.

“It was a fundamental miscalculation Trump did in the outset that the threat of war will compel the Iranians to surrender,” Trita Parsi, head of the Washington, DC-based Quincy Institute, told Al Jazeera. “Instead they fought back, and they fought back very hard.”

The US supply of missile interceptors has fallen low, according to experts like those at the Washington, DC-based Center for Strategic and International Studies. In late July, the centre found it would take at least three years for the Pentagon to bring supplies back to pre-war levels. The White House has denied any such shortage exists , but analysts say the problem is very real, even if it is temporary, and the Pentagon has been forced to redirect resources away from adversaries like China.

That has included US aircraft carriers. The Pentagon has pulled a key asset away from China , dispatching the USS George Washington from Japan to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln in the Gulf, whose sailors have been at sea for months longer than planned because of the war.

Key US bases in the region – including the Navy’s Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain – have been damaged or become unsafe for use, adding hundreds of kilometres to supply lines as ships look as far away as the Indian Ocean island of Diego Garcia for sourcing.

“In my judgement, the US Armed Forces have probably permanently lost access to 15 Persian Gulf bases,” retired US Army four-star general Barry R McCaffrey wrote on X.

“I think it became clear the US is running out of runway on this, so the administration pivoted to what it knows best, or has perceived as effective in the past, which is these economic tools,” said Jamal Abdi, head of the NIAC. “Really, it’s a way for the administration to scale back to where it was before this war but present it as this new enhanced pressure policy.”

‘Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?’

Instead of hitting Iran and others doing business with it, Monday’s sanctions announcement turned out to be little more than yet another warning, analysts say. While the US Department of the Treasury did sanction 60 new individuals and entities from around the globe over their business with Iran, it did not include major Chinese banks or others that help Tehran sell its oil.

At least 90 percent of Iran’s crude oil exports end up in China, netting Tehran tens of billions of dollars in revenue. Ending that trade would need the US to confront China far more directly than it is willing to do. In fact, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent admitted exactly that on Monday, when he responded to a question from reporters about why the US did not immediately announce sanctions on Chinese entities long known to facilitate oil trade.

“Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent responded.

“To me, it’s more a psychological operation than an actual warfare,” Sina Azodi, assistant professor of Middle East Politics at the George Washington University, told Al Jazeera. “It will have an impact, there’s no question, and I’m sure it’s going to scare off people and affect Iran’s economy by creating more chaos and adding uncertainty … but I don’t think it will ultimately change Iranian calculations in the short term.”

Pain for the Iranian people, gain for Washington?

The new US measures seek to expand the scope of already broad restrictions against the Iranian economy, adding the possibility of secondary sanctions against non-Iranian entities dealing with sectors like digital assets, gold, technology, aviation and shipping.

Tensions with Washington have already forced Iranians to contend with things like shortages of medicine and higher fuel prices . Many of the new sectors being targeted are crucial for common Iranians looking to find ways around previous sanctions, analysts point out. Gold can help preserve wealth as the Iranian rial tumbles. Digital assets like cryptocurrencies let relatives send and receive money across borders. Airlines let Iranians visit relatives abroad, or check on loved ones inside the country.

Quincy Institute’s Parsi said he doubts new sanctions would have an impact on the Iranian government, but they will on the Iranian people.

“I think they will likely be quite impactful and painful for the Iranian people,” he said. “But translating that pain into a shift in their policy is a completely different thing.”

He pointed out that the Trump administration has long known how Tehran reacts to attempts to squeeze it economically. During his first term in 2019, Trump was engaged in an online war with Iran, and economic measures tried to exert more pressure on Tehran, prompting Iran-backed Houthi forces to hit tankers in the Gulf as well as oilfields in Saudi Arabia .

Experts say if Iran’s back is against the wall, it will retaliate.

“If the point of these sanctions is to force them to capitulate, then from what we see in the past, the Iranians would rather escalate than capitulate,” Parsi said.

The attempted use of new sanctions will end up further exposing the limits of US power in the conflict, said the Center for International Policy’s Mortazavi.

“The sanctions will deepen the economic pain facing ordinary Iranians. But years of maximum pressure have shown that economic hardship does not automatically translate into political capitulation,” she said. “If anything, this move exposes the limits of the war: Washington can continue raising the costs for Iran, but it has yet to force Tehran to change course.”

Meanwhile, the continued failure to force Iran to give up has not only made the war itself unpopular in the US, but it has also yielded the lowest approval ratings ever for Trump himself, with just 31 percent of Americans supporting the war, and 33 percent approving of the president’s performance, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll.

With US midterm elections just a few months away, that is something leaders in Tehran are well aware of, said George Washington University’s Azodi.

“They calculate ahead of midterm elections in the US that the Trump administration is not going to have an appetite for more conflict,” he said. “Iran is most likely going to try to weather the storm, absorb the pain, until the Trump administration gives them a good offer.”

articles.title: Quote of the day by Aristotle: âThe man of practical wisdom aims at avoiding pain, not at attaining pleasure"
articles.summary: Rest of World News: The pursuit of pleasure is often treated as one of life's simplest goals, but Aristotle offered a more measured view of what it means to live wisely. .
articles.body: The pursuit of pleasure is often treated as one of life's simplest goals, but Aristotle offered a more measured view of what it means to live wisely. In his Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle wrote: âThe man of practical wisdom aims at avoiding pain, not at attaining pleasure.â The statement appears in his discussion of pleasure, pain and self-control, where he considers whether pleasure should be treated as the highest good. Aristotle's argument suggests that practical wisdom is not simply about seeking whatever feels good in the moment. Instead, it involves understanding which desires are worth following and recognising when the pursuit of pleasure can ultimately create greater difficulties. His words remain relevant because modern life constantly encourages people to seek comfort, entertainment and immediate satisfaction. The quote offers a reminder that wisdom can sometimes mean choosing what prevents unnecessary pain rather than constantly pursuing what feels pleasurable.Quote of the day by Aristotle: What did Aristotle mean by the quote?Aristotle's statement centres on the difference between practical wisdom and the pursuit of immediate pleasure. In Nicomachean Ethics, he discusses the way people respond to pleasure and pain and examines the behaviour of those who lack self-control. His point is not that all pleasure is bad or that a wise person should live without enjoyment. Instead, Aristotle distinguishes between pleasures that are beneficial and excessive or misguided pleasures that can lead to problems. The practically wise person therefore does not make pleasure the sole objective. Such a person understands that avoiding unnecessary pain can be more important than chasing temporary enjoyment.The idea becomes clearer when considered alongside Aristotle's broader discussion of self-control. He argues that people can become overly driven by pleasurable things and that this pursuit can itself produce pain. Someone who constantly seeks immediate gratification may eventually face consequences that outweigh the original pleasure. Practical wisdom therefore requires judgement. It means considering where a particular choice will lead rather than evaluating it only by how enjoyable it feels in the present. Aristotle's message is ultimately about moderation, foresight and the ability to place short-term desires within the context of a larger and more balanced life.Why avoiding unnecessary pain can be a form of wisdomPeople often associate wisdom with achieving more, gaining more or experiencing more pleasure. Aristotle's observation presents another way of looking at it. Sometimes the wiser decision is the one that prevents avoidable problems from developing in the first place. A person may choose discipline over excess, restraint over impulse or preparation over convenience because these choices can reduce difficulties later. This does not mean avoiding every challenge. Some difficulties are necessary for growth, and Aristotle's wider philosophy places considerable importance on developing good character through practice and habit. The point is to distinguish between worthwhile difficulty and unnecessary suffering. Practical wisdom helps a person recognise that difference and make choices accordingly.This idea remains relevant in everyday decisions. Eating or spending excessively may provide immediate pleasure but create problems later. Avoiding difficult responsibilities may feel comfortable in the moment but increase stress over time. Similarly, constantly choosing entertainment over meaningful work can offer short-term satisfaction while making long-term goals harder to achieve. Aristotle's argument encourages people to look beyond the immediate emotional reward and consider the consequences of their choices.Why chasing pleasure does not always lead to happinessAristotle's discussion is particularly interesting because he does not simply argue that pleasure is worthless. In Nicomachean Ethics, he examines different arguments about pleasure and ultimately treats pleasure as having an important place in human life. His concern is with the assumption that every pleasurable experience should automatically be pursued. Some pleasures can be excessive, harmful or connected to desires that undermine self-control.This distinction is important in a world where instant gratification is increasingly accessible. Entertainment, shopping, food, social media and other forms of stimulation can provide immediate rewards with very little effort. Yet the fact that something is enjoyable does not necessarily mean that pursuing more of it will improve a person's life. Aristotle's idea encourages a more deliberate approach. Instead of asking only whether something feels good, a person can also ask whether it is good for them, whether it supports their goals and whether the consequences are worth the temporary pleasure.Aristotle and the importance of practical wisdomPractical wisdom, or phronesis, occupies an important place in Aristotle's ethical philosophy. It concerns the ability to deliberate well about how to act in particular circumstances. Rather than relying on simple rules, practical wisdom involves judging what is appropriate in a given situation and choosing actions that contribute to a good life. Aristotle's discussion of pleasure and pain forms part of this wider examination of human behaviour, virtue and self-control.The quote therefore should not be interpreted as a simple instruction to avoid discomfort at all costs. A wise person may willingly accept temporary pain or difficulty when it serves a worthwhile purpose. Studying can be difficult, exercise can be uncomfortable and achieving an important goal can require sacrifice. The wisdom lies in understanding which difficulties are meaningful and which forms of pain are simply the consequences of poor choices. Aristotle's approach asks people to think beyond immediate feelings and consider the broader consequences of their actions.The timeless lessonAristotle's words ultimately encourage a more thoughtful relationship with pleasure and pain. A good life is not necessarily one in which every moment is comfortable or every desire is satisfied. Wisdom involves knowing when to pursue something, when to exercise restraint and when avoiding a particular choice can save us from greater difficulties later. The quote reminds us that self-control is not about rejecting pleasure but about refusing to let pleasure control our decisions. In a culture increasingly focused on instant gratification, Aristotle's ancient observation offers a simple but powerful lesson: sometimes the wisest choice is not the one that promises the greatest pleasure, but the one that prevents unnecessary pain and helps us live with greater balance and judgement.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Best hiking trails near Scott Stadium in Charlottesville: a guide for Virginia football fans
articles.summary: Before the Cavaliers kick off at Scott Stadium, explore Humpback Rocks, the Blue Hole swimming spot, and Shenandoah National Park all within 35 minutes.
articles.body: Week 0 | NC State at Virginia | Saturday, Aug. 29 | Scott Stadium, Charlottesville, VA | 3:30 p.m. ET Funny how things work out. This game was supposed to be college football's first trip to South America, with NC State and Virginia set to kick off Week 0 at Nilton Santos Stadium in Rio de Janeiro. Then the whole thing fell apart this summer when Athlete Advantage (the event organizer) told the ACC it simply couldn't pull it off. So the Wolfpack and Cavaliers got rerouted back to the far less exotic — but far more practical — Blue Ridge foothills of Charlottesville instead. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS Virginia's loss of a trip to Rio is your gain. Instead of fighting for a spot on a flight to Brazil, you can be standing on a mountaintop overlooking the Shenandoah Valley by 9 a.m. and in your tailgate spot by 1. Charlottesville sits right up against the Blue Ridge Parkway and the edge of Shenandoah National Park, which means some of the best hiking in Virginia is closer to Scott Stadium than most fans realize. Here's where to go — all within an hour of kickoff and none requiring a passport or conversational Portuguese. Saunders-Monticello Trail 10 minutes from Scott Stadium | Easy The one to bring the whole crew, including grandparents and strollers. A 4.4-mile out-and-back on packed gravel and raised boardwalk, climbing gently through forest canopy up to the visitor center at Thomas Jefferson's Monticello. Dog-friendly, wheelchair-accessible and shaded most of the way. If anyone in your group wants to actually tour the house, that's a separate ticket — $23 to $30 for adults, $10 for kids 5 to 11 — but the trail itself is free. Blue Ridge Tunnel 30 minutes from Scott Stadium | Easy A change of pace from the usual mountain-view hike: a 4.6-mile out-and-back through an actual 1850s railroad tunnel carved straight through the mountain under Rockfish Gap. Bring a flashlight or headlamp — it gets really dark in there, and the temperature drops the deeper you go, which is an added bonus. BEAT THE HEAT: HERE ARE SOME OF THE BEST TIPS TO AVOID HEATSTROKE DURING A HIKE THIS SUMMER Shenandoah National Park (Rockfish Gap entrance) 25 minutes from Scott Stadium | $30 per vehicle | Moderate If you're only going to spend money on one thing this weekend besides the game, this is the one worth it. The Rockfish Gap entrance drops you right onto Skyline Drive, with two standout hikes an easy detour apart: Calvary and Chimney Rocks at milepost 90, a short trek out to a flat-topped rock overlook, and Turk Mountain at milepost 93.5, which delivers rock scrambles and real mountain views for the effort. Being a national park, it will cost you an entry fee of $30 per vehicle, which is good for seven days. Sugar Hollow Reservoir & the Blue Hole 35 minutes from Scott Stadium | Moderate The pick if you’re looking to do a little soaking. A 3-mile out-and-back from the Sugar Hollow parking area leads to the Blue Hole, a genuinely beautiful swimming hole on the Moormans River. This spot keeps showing up on the "best swimming holes in Virginia" lists for a reason. Bring water shoes; the rocks get slick. If your crew wants more of a workout instead, a separate 4.6-mile route from the same lot heads out to Big Branch Falls through a shaded forest. Humpback Rocks 30 minutes from Scott Stadium | Moderate-strenuous The payoff hike, and the one most worth setting an alarm for. It's a brutal, steep mile straight up, but the reward is a 360-degree view across the Shenandoah Valley and Blue Ridge that's tough to beat anywhere in the state. This is the one hike on the list with zero shade at the top, so this is the one to knock out at sunrise, not after brunch. Sunrise at Humpback is a bucket-list item for many UVA students. Crabtree Falls 60–75 minutes from Scott Stadium | $3 day-use fee | Moderate-strenuous Crabtree Falls is a series of five major cascades tumbling a total of 1,200 feet down the mountainside. For context, that's taller than the Eiffel Tower. And the longest single cascade in that series drops 400 feet, enough to make Crabtree Falls the tallest single vertical-drop waterfall east of the Mississippi. The hike up alongside it is a 3-mile round trip with switchbacks and handrails at the steeper spots. It's genuinely one of the most photographed trails in Virginia. The catch: this one runs 60 to 75 minutes from Scott Stadium depending on route and traffic. If you're rolling into Charlottesville just for the game, Crabtree probably isn't the move. But if you're making a weekend of it and have an extra day before or after, it's worth the drive. We should probably also mention there's another Crabtree Falls off the Blue Ridge Parkway in North Carolina. Make sure you're plugging the right one into your GPS. Truthfully, you can't go wrong no matter which trail you choose. Between the Blue Ridge Parkway, Shenandoah National Park and a reservoir system that seems to have a trail wrapped around every corner of it, Charlottesville is about as good as it gets for outdoor adventurers who also happen to love college football. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Seeking two years to frame creamy layer criteria for OBCs, Centre Tuesday requested Supreme Court for an early hearing on its application against retrospective implementation of SCâs March 11 judgement, which disallowed this classification of OBC candidates based on the salaries of parents employed in PSUs or the private sector.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta requested a bench led by CJI Surya Kant to list the application seeking certain clarifications on the March 11 judgement in the Rohit Nathan case. This was opposed by advocate Varun Thakur, who said the law was settled by SC.The SG said Centre was not seeking review or modification of the judgement but wanted to apprise the court of field-level difficulties in retrospective implementation. The SG said this would require changing the status of older batches of creamy layer OBC candidates to non-creamy and warrant change in cadre, post and service in civil services. It would also necessitate corresponding changes for an equal number of candidates who had long been serving in a cadre and service like IFS, IAS and IPS, and result in chaos.Mehta said he was only requesting early listing before a bench of Justices P S Narasimha and R Mahadevan. CJI agreed to list the applications on Sept 1.In its application, Centre said, âOn account of the serious challenges and implications with the implementation of the directions of SC, govt is committed to bring out a policy which will effectively address the observations made by SC, while also ensuring that the direct and indirect impact of the policy is fair and just.âIf the March 11 judgement is implemented without suitable policy intervention it will have a far-reaching impact on govt recruitments and admissions in higher education institutions undertaken by central as well as 18 state/UT govts, it said.Govt said major bodies/employers â like Railways, banks, the department of posts and paramilitary â would also be flooded with hundreds of thousands of representations/litigations seeking retrospective reclassification of the creamy layer.Following the Indra Sawhney judgement in 1992, govt had issued an office memorandum on Sept 8, 1993, prescribing the criteria for identifying the OBC creamy layer who would be excluded from reservation benefits.In its March 11 judgement, SC had also observed that the determination of the creamy layer status must be based on the occupational categories specified in the 1993 office memorandum and the income of parents employed in private sector organisations could not automatically lead to the conclusion that the candidate belonged to the creamy layer.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Americans' average FICO credit score is holding steady, but experts say this number masks some affordability pressures and reveals how rising costs are shaping their financial decisions.

Today, the average U.S. FICO score sits at 714, down one point from a year ago but unchanged from October 2025, according to a new FICO® Score Credit Insights report.

A FICO credit score is a three-digit number that reflects the information in your credit reports and considers your payment history, amounts owed, credit history length, new credit, and credit mix. This score is used by lenders to make decisions about whether you qualify for mortgages, credit cards, loans, and more.

The report serves as a snapshot of consumers' credit health as rising costs tied to auto loans, housing, and credit cards put pressure on household budgets.

Affordability remains a struggle for many Americans, particularly among lower-scoring and thin-file borrowers.

The report showed that the average monthly payment for a first-time home buyer increased 57% since 2019, and mortgage balances for borrowers with scores below 620 have grown 43% since April 2019.

Auto loan balances for the lowest-scoring borrowers were also up 36%, and subsequent 90-plus-day delinquency rates for both mortgages and autos rose exclusively in the lowest-score bands, remaining flat across all higher score ranges.

"The stability we're seeing in the national average FICO score isn't necessarily because things have gotten easier for consumers — costs have risen across nearly every credit product people use, from mortgages to auto loans to credit cards," said Tommy Lee, senior director at FICO. "What's kept the average steady is that delinquency has actually improved or held steady across every major loan type. That's a story about financial discipline under pressure, not economic ease."

Delinquency remained stable or improved across most products, according to the FICO report. The share of mortgage borrowers in early-stage delinquency eased from 1.42% to 1.35% year over year, while 30-day auto delinquency improved by 5 basis points to 2.6%.

This comes on the heels of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's quarterly report on household debt and credit , which showed that credit card balances rose by $21 billion to stand at $1.26 trillion — a 1.7% increase from the previous quarter and nearing last year's high of $1.28 trillion.

Some of the strategies Americans are using to cover costs include using buy now, pay later services to keep large expenses from straining their budgets and relying on others for ongoing financial support.

Even so, it seems many Americans are still prioritizing their financial health, with nearly three-quarters of Americans checking their FICO scores multiple times a year.

"Younger consumers in particular are treating credit as a tool they're actively managing, not something that happens to them," Lee said. "That said, things have not been easy for younger generations."

He said that about 74% of Gen Z consumers rely on some form of financial support, most often from parents, and, more broadly, 37% of all Americans say the same, with 19% citing parents specifically.

"And 68% of Gen Z homeowners told us housing costs have made it harder to keep up with other expenses," Lee said. "The credit gains are real, but they're happening alongside — not in spite of — meaningful financial strain."

Tips to build and maintain a healthy FICO score

According to FICO, most creditors will consider your scores "good" if they fall between 670 and 739 (on a scale of 300 to 850), with higher scores signaling a lower-risk applicant and lower scores signaling a higher-risk applicant.

Some of the best ways to maintain a healthy score include:

Making payments on time: Payment history is the most heavily weighted factor in your score calculation, so it's important to make payments on time and avoid late or missed payments, defaults, charge-offs, collections, bankruptcies, and foreclosures.

Making more than the minimum payment to reduce your credit utilization : The second most important factor in your FICO score is the amounts owed or how much credit you're using. Working to reduce your balances by making extra payments or paying more than the minimum amount can boost your score.

Limiting new credit applications : Each time you apply for a new credit card or loan, it will result in a hard inquiry. Too many hard inquiries in a short amount of time can negatively impact your score, so it's best to avoid new applications unless absolutely necessary.

articles.title: How Nathan Straus transformed philanthropy and helped make pasteurised milk the safer choice for children
articles.summary: US News: Long before pasteurised milk became a routine part of American life, families in New York faced a serious and often overlooked public-health danger, c.
articles.body: Long before pasteurised milk became a routine part of American life, families in New York faced a serious and often overlooked public-health danger, contaminated milk. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, raw milk could carry harmful pathogens and was especially dangerous for infants and young children. One wealthy businessman, Nathan Straus, used his fortune and business experience to tackle the problem in an unconventional way. Rather than simply donating money to charities, Straus created a system that combined philanthropy with practical retail distribution. He established milk laboratories and depots where pasteurised and refrigerated milk could be sold cheaply or provided free to families who could not afford it. His campaign eventually helped push pasteurisation into mainstream public-health policy and left a lasting mark on how Americans understood safe milk.Nathan Straus turned his business experience towards philanthropyNathan Straus was born in 1848 and became wealthy through his involvement with major New York department stores, including Abraham and Straus and R.H. Macy and Co. After building his fortune, he and his wife, Lina Gutherz Straus, increasingly devoted their attention to philanthropic causes. The New York Public Libraryâs papers document his work in public health, milk pasteurisation, tuberculosis prevention and assistance to people affected by poverty and disasters. Strausâs approach to charity differed from the traditional model of simply handing out money. During the economic depression of the 1890s, he used his experience in merchandising to establish depots near New Yorkâs poorer neighbourhoods, where essential goods could be provided at reduced prices. This practical approach later shaped his campaign for safer milk. His interest in milk became particularly personal and urgent. At the time, milk could spoil during transportation and storage, while contaminated supplies could expose children to dangerous diseases. Straus believed that improving the way milk was processed and distributed could save lives.The milk crisis that put children at riskIn New York City during the 1890s, infant mortality was extraordinarily high. Raw milk was considered one of the major risks because it could contain disease-causing organisms, including bacteria associated with tuberculosis. Although scientists already understood that heating milk could destroy harmful microorganisms, pasteurisation was not yet universally accepted. Straus became one of its most determined advocates. In 1892, he established the Nathan Straus Pasteurized Milk Laboratory in New York at his own expense. The facility produced safer milk and helped establish a distribution network designed specifically to reach families in poorer parts of the city. His milk depots did more than sell a product. They made pasteurised and refrigerated milk accessible to people who might otherwise have had little choice but to purchase cheaper, potentially unsafe supplies. Some milk was sold below wholesale prices, while families unable to pay could receive it without charge. The NYPL collection includes records of the laboratory and its milk depots, including reports, brochures, instructions for mothers, infant-formula recipes and even coupons that could be redeemed at the depots.âRetail givingâ made philanthropy practicalStrausâs method has since been described as a form of âretail givingâ because it applied the efficiency of business to a social problem. Instead of creating a conventional charity dependent entirely on handouts, he developed a system capable of producing, pricing and distributing a health-protective product on a large scale. The approach also included education. Information was provided to mothers about infant care and the safe handling of milk, while doctors and nurses were involved in advising families. Straus supported efforts to demonstrate that pasteurisation could protect children without sacrificing the nutritional value of milk. His work expanded well beyond New York. According to historical accounts of his philanthropy, Straus and his wife ultimately helped establish hundreds of milk stations across numerous American cities. The NYPL collection records his efforts to promote pasteurisation through speeches, articles, medical and public-health meetings, and advocacy for legislation. The strategy was significant because it connected individual access to safer milk with a broader public-health campaign. Families could obtain pasteurised milk immediately, while policymakers and health professionals were exposed to evidence supporting wider adoption.From a private campaign to a public-health standardStrausâs campaign unfolded at a time when public-health officials were increasingly concerned about infant mortality and infectious disease. His work helped demonstrate the practical benefits of making pasteurised milk available to communities that needed it most. The wider movement eventually contributed to changes in public policy. By the early 20th century, pasteurisation was gaining much greater acceptance among American health authorities, and governments increasingly moved towards requiring safer milk supplies. Straus did not single-handedly make American milk safe, but his efforts formed an important part of a much larger public-health transformation. His particular contribution was showing that philanthropy could operate at the point where a public-health problem actually affected people's daily lives: the purchase and consumption of food.A forgotten legacy in American public healthNathan Straus died in 1931, but the records preserved his legacy is striking because the solution he promoted now seems ordinary. Today, consumers generally expect commercially sold milk to have undergone safety controls that were far from universal when Straus began his campaign. What made his philanthropy distinctive was its practical focus. He did not simply ask how much money could be donated to a cause. He asked how a wealthy businessman could use the systems of production, distribution and retail to make a basic necessity safer and more affordable. That approach helped transform milk from a potential source of serious disease into a much safer staple for American families. In doing so, Straus showed how targeted philanthropy could influence not only individual lives but also the development of public-health practices that eventually reached far beyond the people his original milk stations served.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
